title: Mac Finds His Pride

jokes.text: Frank bursts in because the door was unlocked — he dramatically announced he was 'coming in' to a door that was never locked
jokes.setup: Frank pounds on the door urgently, threatens to break it down with great drama
jokes.punchline: "It wasn't locked." The whole dramatic entrance was unnecessary
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank energy — urgent bluster over nothing. The beat lands because it immediately establishes the chaotic, oblivious Frank voice that drives the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Shit. I just opened up the old cut.

jokes.text: "I just opened up the old cut" — Frank's immediate injury upon entering, followed by improvising a nose rag from Mac's sock
jokes.setup: Frank barges in urgently on a mission to help Mac with an emotional crisis
jokes.punchline: He immediately injures himself and starts rummaging for a sock to stuff in his nose wound, completely derailing any gravity
jokes.explanation: This establishes the episode's brilliant running gag: Frank's grotesque physical deterioration becomes a constant absurdist counterpoint to the episode's sincere emotional journey. The 'old cut' implies this is a recurring injury, which is perfectly Frank. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why didn't you open the door?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It wasn't locked.

jokes.text: "We're making a float for the parade, to rope in the gays."
jokes.setup: Frank is tasked with helping organize a gay pride float
jokes.punchline: His framing — 'rope in the gays' — treats LGBTQ people purely as a commercial demographic to be harvested, delivered with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Pure Frank voice: utterly transactional, no malice but zero sensitivity. The Gang's cynical exploitation of Pride is a well-established character trait and this delivers it economically.

dialogue.line: Frank using Mac's sock and newspaper to stuff his wound

jokes.text: "Well, you're gonna be our prize gay. You're gonna dance on top."
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to recruit Mac to help with the float
jokes.punchline: "Prize gay" — treating Mac like a show animal or raffle prize, the most reductive possible framing
jokes.explanation: Compact and character-specific. 'Prize gay' is a genuinely funny phrase that only Frank would use sincerely.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I drew the short straw, so here I am.

jokes.text: "I told 'em, 'I don't get the whole gay thing.' I drew the short straw, so here I am. Let's roll."
jokes.setup: Frank has been sent to help Mac with his emotional crisis about gay identity
jokes.punchline: Frank's complete lack of qualification or desire to help, admitted openly and immediately before demanding they 'roll'
jokes.explanation: Frank's brutal self-awareness about his own uselessness, delivered with zero embarrassment, is a great character beat. 'Let's roll' as the follow-up is perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: And, to be honest, now that you're gay, I get you even less.

jokes.text: "They give me one job and I got to deal with your feelings?"
jokes.setup: Mac expresses genuine emotional vulnerability about not knowing where he fits as a gay man
jokes.punchline: Frank's response treats Mac's existential identity crisis as a mild workplace inconvenience
jokes.explanation: One of the cleaner jokes in the episode. The economy is exceptional — nine words perfectly capture Frank's oblivious selfishness against Mac's genuine emotional pain. The comedic contract between Frank's callousness and Mac's sincerity is what drives the whole episode, and this line crystallizes it perfectly at the outset.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Frank, you're a 75-year-old man with a face that looks like hamburger meat. I'm sure you're safe.

jokes.text: "All right. Look, Mac, I never really got you. And-and, to be honest, now that you're gay, I get you even less."
jokes.setup: Frank is attempting to open up and connect with Mac to help him
jokes.punchline: His version of a bonding speech immediately reveals he understands Mac even less than before — delivered as if this is a helpful insight
jokes.explanation: Frank's attempt at a sincere speech that immediately undercuts itself. The structure is tight: first clause is a confession, second clause is a worse confession delivered as if it's progress. Very Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: This is a much better spread than they have at the straight orgies.

jokes.text: "Nothing against it. I just don't get it." — Frank's attempt at allyship
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to express open-mindedness
jokes.punchline: His disclaimer is the bare minimum of human decency, delivered as if it's a generous concession
jokes.explanation: Slight but functional. Part of the sustained Frank characterization — his 'tolerance' is so tepid it's almost worse than hostility.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Ooh, there must be some hot sauce on them wings. They're buffalo wings.

jokes.text: "Okay. Let's go find your pride." — Frank's mission statement, delivered like a mundane errand
jokes.setup: Mac's crisis is deeply personal and emotional
jokes.punchline: Frank reduces it to a task on his to-do list, like finding his car keys
jokes.explanation: Also the episode title delivered as a punchline. The double meaning (the abstract concept of pride vs. the literal Pride parade) is light but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Mac, unzip this thing, so we can find out what it wants.

jokes.text: "And, by the way, when we're in there, you got to watch my back. If one of these queens comes at me, I'm gonna go berserk."
jokes.setup: Frank and Mac are heading to a gay club so Mac can meet 'normal gays'
jokes.punchline: Frank is terrified of being hit on at a gay bar, as if his 75-year-old hamburger-meat face makes him a target
jokes.explanation: Sets up the next joke perfectly. Frank's delusion that he'd be an object of desire is the implicit joke, made explicit in Mac's response.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Why? Because I'm straight? No. Because you put your nose rags in the chicken.

jokes.text: "Frank, you're a 75-year-old man with a face that looks like hamburger meat. I'm sure you're safe."
jokes.setup: Frank paranoidly worries he'll be hit on and needs Mac to 'watch his back'
jokes.punchline: Mac reassures him with a brutal physical description that demolishes Frank's self-regard while technically being comforting
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The structure is near-perfect: the reassurance IS the insult. 'Face that looks like hamburger meat' is a vivid, specific, memorable image. The deadpan delivery — using a devastating description as comfort — is classic Sunny writing. Highly quotable and efficiently constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Hey, how much I got to pay you to let my boy Mac here take you for a spin?

dialogue.speaker: Leather Man
dialogue.line: I'm not a prostitute.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You do this for fun?

jokes.text: "L-Let's try to blend in." — Frank's reaction upon entering the gay club/sex party
jokes.setup: Frank and Mac enter what turns out to be a leather/BDSM sex club rather than a regular gay bar
jokes.punchline: Frank's instinct is to 'blend in' — implying he thinks he could or would want to
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat. The audience imagines the visual context which does most of the work.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I mean, one false move and these fairies could poke me full of holes.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: 'Fairies'? What year is it in your head?

jokes.text: "Isn't this what all gay guys are into?"
jokes.setup: Mac expresses discomfort at the BDSM sex club Frank has taken him to
jokes.punchline: Frank genuinely believes this is representative of gay culture broadly — maximum ignorance delivered with maximum confidence
jokes.explanation: Frank's confident wrongness is the comedic engine of this whole sequence. He's not homophobic exactly — he just has zero correct information and enormous confidence. The line lands because of the specificity of the setting we're imagining.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: When you came out to your father, did you come out as a top or a bottom? A boy or a girl?

jokes.text: "This is a much better spread than they have at the straight orgies."
jokes.setup: Frank and Mac are at the buffet in the sex club; Frank is scoping the food
jokes.punchline: Frank casually reveals he attends straight orgies with enough regularity to have a basis for comparison — the orgy buffet quality is his primary concern
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and a strong 8+ justified entry. The humor operates on multiple levels simultaneously: Frank attends straight orgies as a septuagenarian (disturbing), he attends them regularly enough to have a comparative baseline (more disturbing), and his takeaway is about food quality (perfectly Frank). The 'better spread' double entendre is likely intentional. This is 100% a Frank joke — no other character could deliver it. It's economic, original, deeply character-specific, and earns a genuine burst laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You're gay and you're dancing with a hot chick who is God?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: The Catholics really fucked you up.

jokes.text: "Go find some nice guys, smack you around a little bit."
jokes.setup: Mac says he doesn't feel comfortable; Frank encourages him to 'jump in headfirst'
jokes.punchline: Frank's idea of a loving push toward connection includes getting physically assaulted as a bonding activity
jokes.explanation: Frank's idea of encouragement being literal violence is on-brand and lands well in context, playing off the BDSM setting.

dialogue.line: Frank's nose swelling and him trying to fix it with insulation

jokes.text: Frank removes bloody nose-stuffing from his face and jams it into the chicken buffet dish to re-plug his wound
jokes.setup: Frank has been using improvised materials (sock, newspaper) to plug a bloody nose cut all episode
jokes.punchline: He removes the soiled plug, sticks it in the chicken to free up his hands, and replaces it — in a sex club's buffet — without apparent concern for other guests
jokes.explanation: High impact because it's viscerally disgusting and visually very funny. The escalation of the nose wound bit pays off here — using it in the food is the natural worst-case outcome. Rewatch bonus because knowing it's coming makes you dread it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.line: My cellmate ratted on me for having an extra pillow. I cut out his tongue with a rusty pair of pliers and fed it to the maggots.

jokes.text: "Ooh, ooh, ooh, that's spicy. Ooh, there must be some hot sauce on them wings." — Frank eats a buffalo wing off the dish containing his bloody nose rag
jokes.setup: Frank has just placed his bloody nose-stuffing in the chicken dish
jokes.punchline: He then eats from that same dish and attributes the unusual taste to hot sauce
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation. We already cringed at the nose rag going in the food; now Frank EATS THE FOOD and compliments the seasoning. The logic is airtight and deeply gross. The 'ooh, ooh, ooh' sells it physically. Strong impact score justified by the full-room cringe-laugh this would generate.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Cool... Very cool.

jokes.text: "Mac, unzip this thing, so we can find out what it wants." — Frank referring to the club's dungeon master/leather-clad figure as an animal or object
jokes.setup: An intimidating costumed figure approaches Frank and Mac
jokes.punchline: Frank's response is to treat the person as an unidentifiable creature that needs to be 'unzipped' to communicate — total dehumanization born of complete ignorance
jokes.explanation: Very funny line. Frank has zero frame of reference for what he's seeing and his solution — unzip it — is both practical and utterly unaware. 'Find out what it wants' treats the person as a stray animal. Very quotable, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.line: My son... finally knocked someone up. I'm gonna be a grandfather.

jokes.text: "No. Because you put your nose rags in the chicken."
jokes.setup: Frank assumes they're being ejected because he's straight
jokes.punchline: The completely reasonable, specific, and mundane actual reason: he contaminated the food
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Frank sets up a victimhood narrative (discrimination) and the actual reason is both completely fair and extremely specific. 'Nose rags' as terminology is funny on its own. The structure is exceptionally clean: misdirection into callback.

dialogue.speaker: Mac's Dad
dialogue.line: My son... finally knocked someone up. I'm gonna be a grandfather.

jokes.text: "Excuse me, Your Highness, I'll be more careful."
jokes.setup: Frank is being told to leave for contaminating the food
jokes.punchline: He responds with sarcastic deference as if the complaint is petty and he's merely agreeing to humor them
jokes.explanation: Functional Frank-ism. The sarcasm of 'Your Highness' implies the nose-rag-in-chicken complaint is unreasonable, which is characteristically delusional Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.line: I never really got you, you know? But now, I see that there's hope for you yet. Well, I-I mean, not with your life, but with the life of your son.

jokes.text: "Hey, how much I got to pay you to let my boy Mac here take you for a spin?"
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to help Mac connect with gay men
jokes.punchline: Frank's version of matchmaking is offering to pay for sexual services, treating the encounter as a pure transaction
jokes.explanation: Frank's total reduction of human connection to commerce. 'Take you for a spin' is an especially degrading phrase applied here, adding to the cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.line: Hey, if it's not a boy, you flush that shit out and try again.

jokes.text: "You do this for fun?" / "I'm never gonna get it. I'll never get this. Why did I get this mission?"
jokes.setup: The person confirms they're not a prostitute — they just enjoy the BDSM lifestyle
jokes.punchline: Frank's existential crisis is triggered not by the BDSM itself but by the idea that someone would do it for free, as if payment would make it sensible
jokes.explanation: Frank's bewilderment at unpaid leisure activity is very specific and funny. The 'mission' callback to his initial framing adds texture.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah. Yeah, definitely. I'll flush that shit out, and you... I'm gonna give you a boy, Dad.

jokes.text: "I mean, one false move and these fairies could poke me full of holes." / "'Fairies'? What year is it in your head?"
jokes.setup: Frank expresses his fear in the drag bar
jokes.punchline: Mac's exasperated correction of Frank's archaic terminology — 'what year is it in your head?' — is a perfect straight-man beat in a show with no straight men
jokes.explanation: Mac's 'what year is it in your head' is a sharp, quotable line. The irony of Mac — who is deeply confused about his own identity — correcting Frank's cultural literacy is a good structural joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: What the hell are you doing?

jokes.text: "When you came out to your father, did you come out as a top or a bottom? A boy or a girl?"
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to help Mac figure out how to come out to his father
jokes.punchline: Frank collapses sexual preference and gender identity into one confused binary, equating 'top/bottom' with 'boy/girl' — revealing a deeply garbled understanding of both
jokes.explanation: Frank's confusion is very specific and unusually creative — merging two entirely different categories into one clumsy question. It's the right kind of wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What are you gonna have you, me, dancing on top of the gay float? No. No, no, the press'll murder us.

jokes.text: "Well, I'm sure there's five or six superviruses eating out your insides." — Frank's response to Mac saying 'you don't know what's going on inside of me'
jokes.setup: Mac says emotionally that Frank doesn't know 'what's going on inside of me'
jokes.punchline: Frank takes it literally and immediately speculates about STIs/disease — completely missing the metaphor
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. The setup is a sincere emotional plea from Mac; Frank's response is to misread the metaphor and pivot to HIV/STI speculation. 'Five or six superviruses' is a hyper-specific, deeply dark, and extremely Frank way to interpret 'what's going on inside me.' The specificity of 'five or six' elevates this above a generic dark joke. Genuinely funny, deeply character-specific, economical and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Allow me to introduce Paddy's top gay, a man everybody in the neighborhood knows, everybody loves. The gay that will rope in all the gays. Cricket.

jokes.text: Mac describes his coming-out vision: a storm, being on his knees, God appearing as 'a very hot chick,' and the two of them dancing
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to explain his complex, Catholic-inflected gay identity to Frank
jokes.punchline: His spiritual metaphor for being gay involves an extremely attractive female God — which confuses everyone including himself
jokes.explanation: This is both funny and profound — Mac's sexuality filtered through his warped Catholic upbringing produces a coming-out metaphor involving a hot female God. It's funny because it's confused and yet completely coherent as a Mac-specific worldview. It also foreshadows the episode's transcendent finale. Exceptional character integration: only Mac's specific cocktail of repression, Catholicism, and identity confusion could produce this.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He looks like a monster, and you look like a monster. We're not trying to invite a bar full of monster men.

jokes.text: "You're gay and you're dancing with a hot chick who is God?" / "The Catholics really fucked you up."
jokes.setup: Mac finishes describing his God-as-hot-chick dancing metaphor
jokes.punchline: Frank summarizes it back with accurate confusion, then delivers the most succinct diagnosis possible
jokes.explanation: "The Catholics really fucked you up" is one of the most quotable lines in the episode and possibly the series. It's a perfect four-word diagnosis of Mac's entire character arc across 13 seasons. Frank's bewildered recap ('You're gay and you're dancing with a hot chick who is God?') is itself funny as a straight repetition of the absurdity. The punchline is economically devastating. Earns 8+ on structure and economy especially.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Frank, it's 2018, and you're the only person who doesn't seem to understand gay culture.

jokes.text: "The Catholics really fucked you up."
jokes.setup: Frank has just processed Mac's vision of God as a sexy dancing woman
jokes.punchline: Frank's summary diagnosis — the Catholics did this — is delivered as a simple statement of fact, the most economical possible response
jokes.explanation: Possibly the most quotable line in the episode after the orgies line. Perfect economy — four words, ten-out-of-ten information density. The humor comes from Frank being completely correct while also being completely the wrong person to offer this diagnosis. It's both a joke about Mac's specific Catholic repression AND a broader cultural observation, delivered as the most obvious thing in the world. Near-perfect economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Lady, I'm not going anywhere until I see an Abraham Lincoln.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Here you go.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: What is this? Like, 73 cents. No. I-I said Abraham Lincoln.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Those are pennies.

jokes.text: Frank attempts to apply something to his infected nose wound in the drag bar — apparently a substance from the bar or makeup table — and it burns and swells
jokes.setup: Frank's nose wound has been progressively worsening throughout the episode
jokes.punchline: He self-medicates with an unknown substance that makes it visibly worse — 'That burns' / 'It's swelling'
jokes.explanation: Part of the sustained Frank wound escalation. Functional cringe comedy — the humor is in how much worse Frank makes things with each intervention.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: No, no, no, no. Lady, I'm not going anywhere until I see an Abraham Lincoln.

jokes.text: "No, no, no, no. I got... I'm using this insulation to plug up the flow."
jokes.setup: Mac points out Frank's nose appears infected
jokes.punchline: Frank dismisses it and reveals he's now using building insulation material as his wound dressing
jokes.explanation: The escalation of increasingly inappropriate wound-stuffing materials (sock → newspaper → insulation) is a solid running gag. Insulation is the right escalation — it's genuinely dangerous and completely absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Like, 73 cents. No. I-I said Abraham Lincoln.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There's a bunch of Lincolns in there. Those are pennies.

jokes.text: "I cut out his tongue with a rusty pair of pliers and fed it to the maggots."
jokes.setup: Luther mentions his cellmate ratted on him — we brace for 'and I reported him' or 'got him transferred'
jokes.punchline: Luther's resolution was horrific torture and mutilation, delivered matter-of-factly
jokes.explanation: The delivery is what makes this. The deadpan, conversational tone applied to graphic torture is pitch-perfect dark comedy. 'Fed it to the maggots' as a specific disposal method elevates it. This tells us everything about Mac's father in one sentence — why Mac is psychologically wrecked, why coming out to him is so terrifying, and why the episode needs to end the way it does.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Frank, it's 2018, and you're the only person who doesn't seem to understand gay culture.

jokes.text: "Cool... Very cool." — Frank's response after Luther describes torturing his cellmate
jokes.setup: Luther has just calmly described cutting out a man's tongue and feeding it to maggots
jokes.punchline: Frank's response — 'Cool... Very cool' — is what you say when someone says they went to Hawaii, not when they describe prison torture
jokes.explanation: One of the best reaction beats in the episode. The two-word response does enormous work: Frank is not shocked because nothing shocks him, he's not approving because he's socially oblivious, he's just moving the conversation along. 'Very cool' as a redundant escalation of the inadequate 'Cool' adds a perfect extra beat. Extremely economic and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Sometimes you got to let the blood flow in order to start the healing. Some cuts you just can't plug up.

jokes.text: Mac's coming-out attempt devolves into the same 'storm inside me / angel woman / dancing' metaphor as before, with Frank visibly trying to interrupt
jokes.setup: Mac is about to come out to his terrifying father; Frank told him to 'rip the Band-Aid off'
jokes.punchline: Mac launches into the same incomprehensible God-as-hot-chick dance metaphor, derailing the whole moment; Frank tries to cut him off
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Mac's inability to just say 'I'm gay' leads him to the same mystical rambling. The audience gets the joke faster this time, which is the right comedic economy for a callback.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: They think they're seeing a Blake Shelton concert, and I put your dad in the front row.

jokes.text: "My son... finally knocked someone up. I'm gonna be a grandfather."
jokes.setup: Mac has been trying to come out as gay; Frank tried to redirect; Luther has heard the metaphor about a woman, dancing, and 'something new being born'
jokes.punchline: Luther interprets the entire coming-out attempt as news of a pregnancy — the worst possible misreading, delivering the opposite outcome Mac wanted
jokes.explanation: The structural peak of the first act. Mac's obscure metaphor — designed to communicate his gayness — perfectly maps onto a pregnancy announcement. The misdirection is earned because Mac's metaphor was genuinely ambiguous. Luther's joy ('I'm gonna be a grandfather') lands as both hilarious and devastating because it's exactly the wrong reaction for the right reasons. The 'finally' implies years of paternal disappointment that Mac has accidentally just resolved with a lie. High structure, high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Unfortunately... Blake Shelton will not be making it today. But, he did send me in his stead, and I've got something special to show you.

jokes.text: "But now, I see that there's hope for you yet. Well, I-I mean, not with your life, but with the life of your son."
jokes.setup: Luther is expressing paternal pride for the first time
jokes.punchline: He immediately clarifies that his hope is not for Mac himself — explicitly not for Mac — but only for the imaginary grandson
jokes.explanation: One of the most precise and devastating lines in the episode. The structure is perfect: sets up genuine paternal warmth, then immediately eviscerates it with a clarification that makes it worse than saying nothing. 'Not with your life' is a brutal four-word dismissal of Mac's entire existence. This is IASIP dark comedy operating at a high level — it's funny because it's perfectly constructed, and it hits because it's true to Luther's character and Mac's wound.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I named him that.

jokes.text: "Hey, if it's not a boy, you flush that shit out and try again."
jokes.setup: Mac tries to note they don't know it'll be a boy
jokes.punchline: Luther's casual eugenics instruction — 'flush that shit out' — delivered as fatherly advice
jokes.explanation: Very dark, very Luther. The casual delivery of a monstrous instruction is pitch-perfect and tells us this man is irredeemable — which contextualizes everything about Mac's psychological damage.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: My name is Ronald McDonald, and...

dialogue.speaker: Mac's Dad
dialogue.line: I named him that.

jokes.text: "Yeah. Yeah, definitely. I'll flush that shit out, and you... I'm gonna give you a boy, Dad."
jokes.setup: Luther instructs Mac to 'flush out' a girl baby
jokes.punchline: Mac enthusiastically agrees to this horrifying proposition in a desperate bid for his father's approval — going further than even affirming the lie, now making active promises
jokes.explanation: Mac going from 'I'm going to come out to my dad' to 'I'll give you a boy, Dad' in one scene is a perfect character collapse. The cringe is both funny and genuinely uncomfortable. The arc of the failed coming-out peaks here before the episode's redemptive finale.

dialogue.speaker: Luther
dialogue.line: My God. I get it.

jokes.text: "This goddamn cut. / I'm using lemon juice and hot glue to close up the wound."
jokes.setup: Frank's nose wound has been escalating all episode (sock, newspaper, insulation)
jokes.punchline: Frank is now using lemon juice and hot glue — not only ineffective but actively terrible medical choices — with the same casual confidence
jokes.explanation: The escalation is working perfectly — each material is worse than the last. Lemon juice (acidic, would burn an open wound) plus hot glue (a craft supply) is a genuinely creative escalation. Frank's calm delivery of this insane medical plan is very funny.

jokes.text: The Gang reveals the float — it has a working bar, confetti cannons, and a shower that will pour water on Mac during his 'sexy gay dance or whatever the hell he's been working on'
jokes.setup: The Gang needs Mac to dance on the float for commercial reasons
jokes.punchline: The float is elaborate and thoughtful, but their description of Mac's contribution — 'his sexy gay dance or whatever the hell he's been working on' — reveals they have zero understanding of or interest in what Mac is actually doing
jokes.explanation: Functional Gang-dynamics joke. The contrast between their investment in the float infrastructure and their dismissal of Mac's emotional contribution is consistent character work.

jokes.text: Frank returns to Mac's apartment and finds a woman there — 'Who the hell are you?'
jokes.setup: Frank left Mac alone and returns, expecting to find him ready to go
jokes.punchline: Mac has found a woman — presumably attempting to fulfill his father's expectation — and Frank walks in on this
jokes.explanation: The discovery beat works as a visual punchline — Frank's expression walking in on Mac with a woman while trying to help him embrace being gay is an effective joke told almost entirely through implication.

jokes.text: Mac says 'No.' in response to Frank's accusation — a single-word denial of the obvious
jokes.setup: Frank has clearly walked in on Mac with a woman
jokes.punchline: Mac's single 'No.' is a completely unconvincing denial
jokes.explanation: The economy of one word as a denial is good. It's the character equivalent of a child denying they ate the cookie with chocolate on their face.

jokes.text: "I can't stand it. Nobody can stand it." — Frank's reaction to the idea of Mac going back in the closet
jokes.setup: Frank accuses Mac of going back in the closet; Mac denies it
jokes.punchline: Frank's objection to the closet isn't rooted in care for Mac's wellbeing — it's personal annoyance. 'Nobody can stand it' implies the Gang has collectively suffered from Mac's closeted years
jokes.explanation: Frank's concern for Mac is entirely selfish — the closet was inconvenient for HIM. 'Nobody can stand it' is a great line because it reframes years of Mac's internal struggle as everyone else's social burden.

jokes.text: Frank introduces Cricket as 'Paddy's top gay, a man everybody in the neighborhood knows, everybody loves. The gay that will rope in all the gays.'
jokes.setup: Frank needs to replace Mac on the float with someone authentically gay
jokes.punchline: Frank's replacement is Cricket — the Gang's homeless, disfigured, frequently victimized punching bag — presented with PR-level superlatives
jokes.explanation: Cricket's reveal is well-earned. The setup of Frank promising 'somebody way hotter than Mac' followed by Cricket is a classic misdirection. 'Everybody in the neighborhood knows, everybody loves' applied to Cricket — who is literally a neighborhood disaster — is perfect ironic framing. His laugh ('Ha, ha, ha') is a great character beat.

jokes.text: "He looks like a monster, and you look like a monster. We're not trying to invite a bar full of monster men."
jokes.setup: Frank presents Cricket as the replacement gay dancer
jokes.punchline: Dennis flatly tells Frank and Cricket that both of them look like monsters — no softening, no hedge
jokes.explanation: The Gang insulting Cricket is a franchise staple but 'monster men' as the category is fresh. Including Frank in the same 'monster' bracket as Cricket is Dennis operating at peak cruelty. 'We're not trying to invite a bar full of monster men' is a very quotable line.

jokes.text: "Frank, it's 2018, and you're the only person who doesn't seem to understand gay culture."
jokes.setup: The Gang is trying to explain why Frank can't be the face of gay outreach
jokes.punchline: The year call-out combined with the specific accusation lands as both a joke and a meta-comment on the show's own evolution re: Mac's gayness
jokes.explanation: The 'it's 2018' line is lightly meta — the show itself took 13 seasons to get here, and this is a wink at that. Functions as both in-universe comedy and mild self-awareness.

jokes.text: "That's true. That's true. My head is swelling with blood."
jokes.setup: Dennis accuses Frank of not understanding gay culture; Frank concedes
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately pivots from agreeing to noting his head is 'swelling with blood' — the wound update is delivered as a natural continuation of the conversation
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'you're right, I don't understand gay culture' to 'my head is swelling with blood' is perfectly timed and absolutely Frank. The nonchalant medical update mid-argument is very funny.

jokes.text: "Lady, I'm not going anywhere until I see an Abraham Lincoln."
jokes.setup: Cricket is being recruited to dance on the float, presumably for pay
jokes.punchline: Cricket demands payment in the form of an 'Abraham Lincoln' — referring to a $5 bill — with the gravity of a business negotiation
jokes.explanation: Cricket's rock-bottom price point (he's negotiating for $5) combined with the formal 'Abraham Lincoln' phrasing creates a beautiful character joke. His dignity in demanding payment is perfect Cricket: maintaining performative self-respect at the absolute floor of desperation.

jokes.text: "What is this? Like, 73 cents." / "Those are pennies."
jokes.setup: Cricket demanded an 'Abraham Lincoln' ($5 bill)
jokes.punchline: Dee pays him with literal pocket change — 73 cents in pennies — and Cricket identifies the problem with precision before the audience can
jokes.explanation: 'Those are pennies' is a very good punchline — Cricket's patient correction ('No. I-I said Abraham Lincoln. There's a bunch of Lincolns in there. Those are pennies.') shows he has standards even at the lowest rung. The sequence has good structure and escalates the Cricket-dignity joke well.

jokes.text: "Okay, 'Start north on Second Street. Turn right on... Dickens Avenue.'"
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to figure out how to drive the float using GPS navigation
jokes.punchline: The GPS directions include 'Dickens Avenue' — a crude joke hidden in the navigation directions
jokes.explanation: A cheap wordplay gag that feels a little below the show's usual standard. It gets a mild laugh from the placement (pride parade GPS) but it's a rude-word-in-a-name joke, which is fairly low-craft. Not harmful but not strong either.

jokes.text: Frank attempts to drive the float, immediately struggles, says 'This is ridiculous. Shit, I can't do this. Screw this.'
jokes.setup: Frank confidently takes over driving the float
jokes.punchline: He immediately fails and gives up — the same energy as his confidence in every other area of the episode
jokes.explanation: Functional physical comedy beat. Frank's immediate incompetence is consistent but this iteration doesn't add much new information. Gets a mild laugh from his frustration but isn't a strong joke.

jokes.text: Frank uses his own bloody wound as a metaphor for Mac's emotional state — 'sometimes you got to let the blood flow in order to start the healing. Some cuts you just can't plug up.'
jokes.setup: Frank has been physically bleeding all episode while trying to help Mac come out emotionally
jokes.punchline: The running gag culminates in Frank using his grotesque medical situation as a sincere metaphor — and it actually works as advice, which is the final ironic twist
jokes.explanation: This is the thematic and comedic masterpiece of the episode. The entire Frank-wound running gag — which seemed like pure absurdist gross-out humor — was secretly being built as a physical metaphor for Mac's emotional repression. The payoff is that Frank's terrible, bloody advice about 'letting it flow' is CORRECT and SINCERE and also comes from a man literally dripping blood on the floor. The earned vs. cheap score is high because this takes 13 minutes of setup to land properly. This is what IASIP does at its best: lowbrow physical comedy that secretly carries emotional truth.

jokes.text: "They think they're seeing a Blake Shelton concert" — the cover story Frank gave prison inmates
jokes.setup: Frank has somehow arranged for Mac to perform for his father and the prison population
jokes.punchline: The prisoners were told they'd see Blake Shelton — a country star with no apparent connection to anyone in the story — and are about to see Mac's interpretive gay coming-out dance instead
jokes.explanation: Blake Shelton is a perfect choice — mainstream, non-threatening country star, completely incongruous with what's about to happen. The specificity of the choice (not 'a concert,' not a cool artist — Blake Shelton) is very funny. The audience imagines a prison full of men expecting 'God's Country' and getting Mac's spiritual interpretive dance.

jokes.text: "My name is Ronald McDonald, and... I named him that." — Frank's aside to the audience/prison crowd about Mac's name
jokes.setup: Mac introduces himself by his full name — Ronald McDonald — to the prison audience
jokes.punchline: Frank breaks in to claim credit for naming him — a non-sequitur aside that reveals the absurd backstory of Mac's real name, delivered with quiet pride
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words, 'I named him that,' delivered with zero self-awareness about naming a child after a fast food mascot, breaking the emotional momentum of the scene with quiet absurdist pride. It's the last laugh before the episode pivots to pure emotion, and it lands perfectly as a grace note.

jokes.text: Mac announces to the prison: 'Unfortunately, Blake Shelton will not be making it today. But he did send me in his stead.'
jokes.setup: An entire prison population believes they're seeing Blake Shelton
jokes.punchline: Mac announces the cancellation while implying he is Blake Shelton's representative/replacement — to a prison crowd
jokes.explanation: 'He did send me in his stead' is a beautiful formal phrase to use while delivering this news to prisoners expecting a country music star. The understated politeness of the announcement is very funny.

jokes.text: Mac declares 'Dad... I'm gay.' to a prison full of men who thought they were seeing Blake Shelton
jokes.setup: Frank told the prisoners they're seeing Blake Shelton
jokes.punchline: Mac's coming-out is being delivered to an involuntary audience of prisoners who have no choice but to watch
jokes.explanation: The irony is rich: Mac's most private moment is delivered to the least willing audience possible. The situational irony is strong even as the episode pivots away from pure comedy toward genuine emotion.

jokes.text: 'I get it.' — Frank
jokes.setup: Frank has said 'I don't get it' / 'I'll never get it' repeatedly throughout the episode
jokes.punchline: 'I get it.' — three words that complete the episode's comedic and emotional arc simultaneously
jokes.explanation: One of the most economical callbacks in IASIP history. The entire episode has been structured around Frank not understanding — gay culture, Mac's feelings, the metaphor, all of it. 'I get it.' at the end is both the comedic payoff to every 'I don't get it' joke AND the emotional resolution of the episode. Three words. The structure is flawless: an episode-length setup paid off with maximum economy. This is craft at the highest level.

tmdb_overview: Frank tries to recruit Mac for the gang’s kickass float for the Gay Pride Parade. It dawns on Frank that Mac will never be secure with his sexual identity unless he comes out to his father.
